statements.body: The project is named Refill Nudge.
The operator is a single pharmacist running a small independent pharmacy.
A pharmacy technician handles prescription pickup on behalf of the pharmacy.
The core function is to remind patients when their repeat prescriptions are due for refill.
Accuracy is prioritised over coverage: no reminder is preferable to a wrong reminder.
What channels will be used to deliver reminders to patients (e.g. SMS, email, phone call, app notification)?
What data source holds current prescription and dispensing records (e.g. existing pharmacy management system, manual records)?
What defines 'due for refill' — a fixed day count before estimated run-out, a refill eligibility date from the prescriber, or something else?
What patient consent or opt-in mechanism is required before sending reminders?

concerns.coverage: Patients miss timely refills of repeat prescriptions because they are not reminded; the pharmacy operator wants an automated nudge system to close that gap.

The pharmacist is the sole operator; the pharmacy technician is a secondary actor handling pickup; patients are the beneficiaries receiving reminders. Pharmacy scale is small and independent, implying a low patient volume relative to a chain.

A wrong reminder (incorrect timing or wrong patient) could cause a patient to miss a medication dose; the operator has explicitly chosen a conservative policy of suppressing uncertain reminders rather than risking a bad one.
Correctness of reminder timing is the primary quality bar; the operator has stated a zero-tolerance stance on false reminders, accepting lower recall in exchange for higher precision.

candidates.body: Walk me through the intended path of a single reminder: when a repeat prescription approaches its due date, what happens from detection to the patient receiving the nudge, and does the pharmacist review or approve reminders before they go out?
candidates.whySelected: Workflow is an uncovered core concern, and the answer directly operationalises the approved accuracy-over-coverage policy — a human-review step versus fully automatic sending is the single biggest design fork for the first slice.

candidates.body: What observable outcome would tell you Refill Nudge is working — for example, fewer late pickups, fewer lapsed repeats, or less time spent phoning patients?
candidates.whySelected: Success is the other uncovered core concern; without an observable target the conservative suppression policy has no counterweight and the tool could silently send almost nothing while appearing 'safe'.

candidates.body: When a reminder is suppressed because the system is unsure, should anyone — you or the technician — be told, or is silent suppression acceptable?
candidates.whySelected: This bounds the workflow around the already-ratified precision-first policy and prevents suppressed reminders from becoming an invisible failure mode, but it is narrower than the end-to-end workflow question.

readyAdvice.why: Two core concerns (workflow and success) are uncovered, and four ratified unknowns — delivery channel, data source, refill-due definition, and consent — remain open. The first vertical slice cannot be bounded until at least the workflow path and data source are answered.

statements.body: Reminder scheduling is triggered at the point of dispensing a repeat prescription, not by a separate review step.
The reminder is scheduled to fire a few days before the estimated refill date; the exact day offset is not yet defined.
When the patient picks up the prescription, the technician marks the reminder as done, closing the reminder loop.
Reminders are sent without pharmacist pre-approval; the system fires automatically based on the dispense-time schedule.

concerns.coverage: A repeat dispense event triggers reminder scheduling; the reminder fires a few days before refill date; the technician marks the item done at pickup. No manual pharmacist approval step exists in this path.
The dispense event and refill date are the inputs needed to schedule a reminder; the technician's pickup confirmation is a state transition that must be recorded to suppress or close the reminder.

candidates.body: What observable outcome would tell you Refill Nudge is working — for example fewer late refills, fewer patient calls chasing prescriptions, or a target percentage of on-time pickups?
candidates.whySelected: Success is the only uncovered core concern; without an observable success signal there is no way to judge whether the conservative reminder policy is actually helping patients.

candidates.body: Given that reminders fire automatically with no pharmacist approval, what check or condition must a scheduled reminder pass before sending so that an uncertain one is suppressed rather than sent wrong?
candidates.whySelected: The ledger commits to both fully automatic sending and a no-wrong-reminders policy; naming the suppression rule is what makes those two decisions compatible and bounds the first slice's safety logic.

candidates.body: How is the estimated refill date calculated from a dispense event — days' supply dispensed, prescriber's eligibility date, or something else?
candidates.whySelected: The schedule fires relative to an estimated refill date, but the ledger records the definition of 'due for refill' as an open unknown; the timing logic cannot be built until this is answered.

contradictions.summary: Reminders are sent fully automatically with no pharmacist pre-approval, yet the operator's policy is that no reminder is preferable to a wrong one; without a defined suppression or validation rule, automation has no mechanism to honour the accuracy-over-coverage stance.
Reminder timing is anchored to an estimated refill date a few days out, but the definition of 'due for refill' is still an approved unknown, so the anchor the schedule depends on is undefined.

readyAdvice.why: The success concern is entirely uncovered, and two live tensions — the missing suppression rule for automatic sends and the undefined refill-date calculation — leave both the safety policy and the core scheduling logic unbuildable. Resolving these three points would likely make the seed ready for a first slice.

statements.body: All patient data — names, phone numbers, and medication names — must remain stored on the pharmacy's local computer; no data may be sent to or stored in any cloud service.
Patient names, phone numbers, and medication names are classified as sensitive data within this system.

concerns.coverage: Patient names, phone numbers, and medication names are the sensitive data fields held by the system; all data must remain on the pharmacy's local computer with no cloud storage or transmission.
The system must run entirely on-premises on the pharmacy's existing computer; cloud hosting, cloud storage, and cloud processing are hard constraints excluded from any solution.
In addition to reminder accuracy risk, data residency is a safety concern: patient PII and medication names must not leave the local machine, ruling out any SaaS or cloud-connected delivery path.

candidates.body: Given that all patient data must stay on the local machine, how can a reminder physically reach a patient — does sending an SMS or email (which transmits a name, phone number, or medication reference through an external carrier) count as data leaving the machine, or is transient transmission for delivery acceptable?
candidates.whySelected: This resolves the sharpest tension in the ledger: the core function requires delivering a message to a patient, but the approved constraint forbids data leaving the local computer. Until the user says whether transmission-for-delivery is exempt, the channel question is unanswerable and no delivery path can be designed.

candidates.body: What observable evidence would tell you Refill Nudge is working — for example, fewer late refills, patients mentioning the reminder at pickup, or a count of reminders that led to on-time pickups?
candidates.whySelected: Success is the only uncovered core concern; without an observable outcome the framing cannot close, and the answer also shapes what the system must record (e.g. pickup timing) in the first slice.

candidates.body: Since reminders fire automatically with no pharmacist approval, what conditions should cause the system to suppress a reminder rather than send it (e.g. missing days' supply, prescription changed since dispense, patient marked as picked up)?
candidates.whySelected: The approved zero-tolerance stance on wrong reminders sits uneasily with fully automatic sending; naming the suppression conditions is how that safety policy becomes enforceable in the first slice.

contradictions.summary: The core function is to send reminders to patients, but the hard constraint says no patient data (names, phone numbers, medication names) may be sent off the local machine; any SMS, email, or call inherently transmits some of that data through external infrastructure.

The operator prefers no reminder over a wrong one, yet reminders fire fully automatically with no pharmacist pre-approval, leaving no defined mechanism that enforces the accuracy-over-coverage policy.

readyAdvice.why: The success concern is still uncovered, and the delivery-versus-local-only tension blocks the single most important design decision (how a reminder reaches a patient at all). Resolving that tension and naming an observable success signal are both needed before the first slice is bounded.

statements.body: Reminder messages must not state the dosage or medication name; they may only indicate that a refill is due.
When a patient record is unclear or ambiguous, the system must suppress the reminder entirely rather than send a potentially incorrect one.

concerns.coverage: Transient transmission for delivery was the open question; the operator resolved it by restricting message content to non-clinical language (refill due only, no dosage or medication name), which reduces the sensitivity of transmitted data. The nightmare case is a wrong-dosage or wrong-patient reminder, addressed by content restriction and suppression on ambiguity.

Suppression on ambiguous records is now an explicit quality rule: any uncertainty in the underlying record must produce no reminder, reinforcing the precision-over-recall stance with a concrete trigger condition.

candidates.body: What observable change would tell you Refill Nudge is working — for example, fewer patients arriving days late for refills, a target percentage of on-time pickups, or something else you can count at the counter?
candidates.whySelected: Success is the only uncovered core concern; without an observable measure the pharmacist cannot judge whether the precision-over-recall policy is actually helping patients or silently suppressing too many reminders.

candidates.body: What system or record currently holds your dispensing data — a pharmacy management system with an accessible database or export, or paper/manual records?
candidates.whySelected: This is an approved but unanswered unknown; the answer determines whether dispense-time triggering is technically feasible on the local machine and heavily bounds what the first vertical slice can build against.

candidates.body: Which single delivery channel should the first version use to send the non-clinical 'refill due' message — SMS, email, or an automated phone call?
candidates.whySelected: Channel is an approved unknown; now that message content has been restricted to non-clinical language, choosing one concrete channel unblocks the delivery half of the first slice.

readyAdvice.why: Success remains an uncovered core concern, and two ratified unknowns (data source and delivery channel) still block the first vertical slice; the safety and quality posture is well established, but the seed cannot bound a buildable slice until the data source is known.

statements.body: Success is defined as a noticeable drop in late pickups within two months of deployment.
A two-month observation window is long enough to detect a meaningful change in late-pickup frequency at this pharmacy's patient volume.

concerns.coverage: A noticeable reduction in late pickups within two months is the observable evidence of project success; no specific numeric threshold has been set, but the operator expects the change to be visible at the counter.

candidates.body: What system currently records your dispensing events — a pharmacy management software package, a spreadsheet, or paper — and can the reminder tool read from it automatically?
candidates.whySelected: The whole workflow hinges on the dispense event as the trigger (b2658193), but the ledger's own unknown (bc6bbd66) about where dispensing records live is still open. Whether the source is an existing pharmacy management system with a readable database, a spreadsheet, or paper determines whether dispense-time triggering is an integration, an export job, or a manual entry step — three very different first slices. Nothing else in the ledger can be built until this is answered.

candidates.body: Which single delivery channel should the first version use to send the refill-due message — SMS, email, or an automated phone call?
candidates.whySelected: The channel unknown (49f89364) is still open even though the transmission-sensitivity question was resolved: content is now restricted to non-clinical language, but the mechanism itself is unchosen. On a local-only machine, SMS typically needs a modem or carrier gateway while email needs an outbound mail path, so the choice shapes hardware, cost, and the delivery half of the first slice.

candidates.body: How will patients opt in to receiving reminders — a form at the counter, verbal consent recorded by the technician, or something else?
candidates.whySelected: Consent (8d436fdc) is an open unknown with regulatory weight: sending automated messages to patient phone numbers without recorded opt-in could itself be the wrong-reminder harm the operator wants to avoid. It bounds the slice less than the data-source or channel questions, but it must be answered before the first real message is sent.

readyAdvice.why: All ten core concerns have coverage and the safety posture is well defined, but two ledger unknowns block a buildable first slice: the dispensing data source (bc6bbd66) and the delivery channel (49f89364). Until those are answered, the trigger side and the delivery side of the reminder path are both unimplementable. Answering the data-source question first is advised, as it constrains everything downstream.
